opus-5.5.text:
I think what's really fascinating about co-scientist is that it isn't just a single model answering a question. It mirrors the way science actually gets done. When you think about how a research community works, you have people proposing hypotheses, others critiquing them, people debating, refining ideas, ranking which directions are most promising, and then iterating. Science is a deeply collaborative and adversarial process at the same time.

What we tried to do was take that structure and instantiate it with Gemini playing different roles. You have agents that generate hypotheses, agents that review and critique them, and agents that compare ideas against each other in something like a tournament, where hypotheses are debated head to head and the stronger ones rise. Then there are agents that take the best ideas and evolve them, combine them, or push them in new directions. A supervisor coordinates all of this and decides where to spend compute.

The interesting insight for me is that you get a kind of test-time scaling for reasoning. The more you let the system think, debate, and refine, the better the quality of the hypotheses gets. It's not just retrieving what's in the literature; it's synthesizing across it and producing novel, testable ideas.

And crucially, the scientist stays in the loop. The goal isn't to replace the researcher. It's to give them a tireless collaborator that can read far more than any human could, generate many candidate directions, and stress-test them, so the scientist can focus on judgment, taste, and the experiments. When some of the hypotheses it proposed were independently validated in the lab, that was a really exciting moment, because it suggested this kind of system could genuinely accelerate discovery.

r001.rationale: The response says Gemini plays different roles through agents, but does not state that differently prompted Gemini models perform those roles.

r002.rationale: It says debate and refinement improve hypothesis quality, but does not clearly compare the combined system’s proposals against those from a single Gemini model.

fable-5.1.text:
What I find most interesting is that we didn't try to build one big model that magically spits out hypotheses. We looked at how science actually happens in a good lab, and that process is not a single step. A scientist reads the literature, forms an idea, and then that idea gets taken apart by colleagues. Someone says the mechanism doesn't make sense, someone points out a paper from 2015 that already tried this, someone proposes a variant that might work better. The idea that survives is the one that survives that argument.

So the co-scientist is really a system of Gemini-based agents that play those roles. There is generation, where agents go out, read the literature, and propose hypotheses. There is reflection, where other agents critique them, check them for novelty and for whether they are grounded in known biology or chemistry. There is a tournament, where hypotheses are compared against each other in a kind of debate and ranked. And then there is evolution, where the promising ones get refined, combined, or simplified, and the cycle runs again. A supervisor agent allocates compute across all of that.

The reason this matters is that it gives you a self-improving loop. You can give the system more time, more compute, and the quality of what comes out at the end actually gets better, because it has run more rounds of critique and revision. That is closer to how a research group works than to how a chatbot works.

The other thing that struck me is how important the scientist in the loop remains. The system doesn't replace the researcher. The researcher sets the goal in natural language, can inject their own ideas into the tournament, and can push back on the system's reasoning. In the work we did with collaborators on things like drug repurposing for leukemia or the mechanism of antimicrobial resistance, the exciting moment was when the system arrived at something the experts had worked out independently but hadn't yet published. That told us the process was capturing something real about scientific reasoning, not just pattern matching on text.

r001.rationale: It describes Gemini-based agents playing different scientific roles, but does not say they are differently prompted.

r002.rationale: It says quality improves through more rounds of critique and revision, but does not clearly state that the multi-agent system produces better proposals than a single Gemini model.

astra-6.text:
What I find particularly interesting is that it’s not just asking Gemini to come up with an idea. It’s using Gemini in different roles to create a process: propose a hypothesis, critique it, compare it with alternatives, and then refine it. That interaction is a big part of how science works. An idea becomes stronger because someone challenges its assumptions or offers a different explanation.

And that gives the system a way to spend more time working on a problem, rather than treating the first answer as the final answer. It can explore different directions and use those critiques to improve its proposals.

But the crucial distinction is that a compelling hypothesis is still a hypothesis. You need experiments to establish whether it’s right. So I see the value as helping scientists explore possibilities and identify promising experiments, with the scientist guiding the process and the evidence ultimately deciding.

r001.rationale: The response describes Gemini taking different roles, but does not say those roles are carried out by differently prompted models.

r002.rationale: It says critique and exploration can improve proposals, but does not claim the combined multi-agent system produces better proposals than a single Gemini model.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find particularly interesting is that it’s not just asking Gemini to come up with an answer. It’s using Gemini to bring different parts of the scientific process together: generating hypotheses, critiquing them, comparing alternatives, and then refining the most promising ideas.

In science, an idea gets stronger through that back-and-forth. You propose something, a colleague points out a weakness, and you go back and rethink it. The co-scientist system tries to create that kind of interaction, with different agents taking on different roles.

And the goal is to give the scientist something useful to test. A hypothesis can sound very compelling and still be wrong. So that connection back to experiments, and to the scientist’s judgment about which experiments are worth doing, is really important.
